Russia and Ukraine trade huge overnight strikes hours after Moscow agrees to resume peace talks
items.summary:
Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, just hours after talks in St. Petersburg raised hopes of movement toward peace. Kyiv authorities said the Russian strikes wounded 15 people and damaged subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River, and an earlier attack on Wednesday evening had wounded six more people in the capital.

Ukraine answered with a huge drone wave of its own. Moscow's mayor said 630 drones were sent toward the Russian capital, most of them shot down at long range, with two people wounded near Moscow. In the Kharkiv region a Russian strike killed a woman and injured four others, and a drone hit energy infrastructure near Kremenchuk, a major industrial hub.

The fighting sits uneasily beside the diplomacy. After envoy Steve Witkoff called his meeting with President Putin constructive, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia is ready in principle to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the United States, possibly around November 10 in Abu Dhabi. President Zelenskiy has said Ukraine could accept freezing the war along the current front line as a starting point.

Watch whether the Abu Dhabi date firms up — and whether either side slows the strikes while it does.

items.title: U.S. and Israel are planning a possible attack on Iran after the midterm elections, sources say
items.summary:
The United States and Israel are preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran in early November, after the November 3 midterm elections, a person briefed on the planning told NPR on Thursday. American forces are being gathered in the region to be ready by then, though the preparations could also be intended as pressure for a diplomatic deal.

According to the reporting, Israel had initially planned a strike in mid-October, ahead of its own October 27 elections, but President Trump objected. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking re-election while campaigning on a threat to topple Iran's government. Parallel reporting describes a short, intense operation of about three days aimed at nuclear facilities, missile and drone stockpiles and energy sites.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Thursday that Tehran is prepared for diplomacy and for war, and that any scenario — including an attack — is conceivable. The White House would not comment on plans, while saying the president wants to keep Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.

Nothing has been approved yet, and the buildup may still be leverage. Watch for official denials or confirmations, and for movement in oil prices, which are already climbing on the tension.

items.title: Paris bans protests in the centre as Macron accuses Trump of exploiting France's unrest
items.summary:
Paris police banned protests across much of the city centre on Thursday, from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., covering the Élysée Palace, parliament, the Louvre and the Champs-Élysées, plus the Bastille and République squares and the Châtelet-Les Halles shopping district that looters hit hard over the weekend. Student demonstrations were also banned in Paris and Lyon.

The ban follows Saturday's nationwide cost-of-living marches, which drew more than half a million people after four weeks of student protests, and the worst rioting France has seen in years. The justice minister said 174 people have been jailed and 917 prosecuted out of about 2,500 taken into custody, and several cities are keeping curfews that officials credit with calming the streets.

President Emmanuel Macron, speaking in Doha, accused foreign leaders — pointing at President Trump without naming him — of campaigning at France's expense. Trump has linked the unrest to immigration on the campaign trail, while far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads polling for the 2027 presidential race, called Macron's remarks conspiratorial.

Markets are part of the story now: France's 10-year borrowing cost passed 5% on debt worries, and a Moody's decision on French debt is expected Friday. Unions are planning strikes early next month.

items.title: Beatings, spyware and threats darken Serbia ahead of Sunday's election, Reuters finds
items.summary:
Serbians vote on Sunday in an election that could extend Aleksandar Vucic's 12 years in power, as he runs for prime minister. A Reuters investigation, built on interviews with activists, student protesters and opposition figures, describes an increasingly authoritarian climate of routine threats, shrinking press freedom and rising corruption — a picture Vucic and his party deny.

The challenge comes from an unexpected place. The student protest movement that grew out of the November 2024 Novi Sad station collapse, which killed 16 people, is fielding 250 of its own candidates, and a poll this week put the students level with Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party.

Reuters also documented digital and physical pressure. A digital-rights group counted 14 people targeted with advanced spyware, including cases forensic testers linked to Pegasus, and the investigation recounts beatings at protests, including one in Valjevo captured on verified video. Serbia's press-freedom ranking has fallen to 104th of 180 countries, its lowest ever.

Sunday's result will show whether the student movement can turn street protest into parliamentary power. Watch the turnout among younger voters.

items.title: Government websites go dark worldwide after an AI-found flaw in a core web language sparks a scramble
items.summary:
Government websites across Europe and beyond were taken offline on Wednesday after researchers disclosed two critical flaws in PHP, the programming language behind much of the web. The bugs, scored 9.2 out of 10 and nicknamed PHP2Shell, can let an attacker run code remotely without logging in — and they had been sitting in the code since 2012.

What makes the episode unusual is how the flaws were found: with artificial intelligence. Security firms say large language models helped surface the vulnerabilities, and Amazon says it detected an attempt to exploit a decoy system on October 17, days before the public disclosure, with broader exploitation attempts following on Wednesday.

The scale explains the scramble. PHP powers roughly three-quarters of websites whose technology can be identified, including WordPress, Drupal and Joomla sites, and analysts counted about 1.5 million servers running versions with no fix available. The Dutch cyber security centre, Finland's state IT provider, France's Interior Ministry and Wikipedia were among those that took systems offline as a precaution.

Patched PHP versions are now available, and site owners are being urged to update immediately. Watch how many sites remain unpatched in the coming days — that gap is where the damage would happen.

items.title: New U.S.-backed Southeast Asia undersea cable shuts out China as it picks a supplier
items.summary:
A new U.S.-backed undersea data cable linking Malaysia, Vietnam, Singapore and Thailand will choose its supplier this month — and Chinese companies are not in the running. The developers told Reuters the choice is between Japan's NEC and France's Alcatel Submarine Networks, after the American bidder declined because of existing commitments.

The cable, called MViSTA, would run about 2,500 kilometres with 16 fibre pairs, cost roughly $400 million, and enter service in late 2028. Its route was designed to avoid the wide area Beijing claims in the South China Sea, and the linked data-centre campus in southern Vietnam will use no Chinese technology in key roles, its backers say.

Washington is involved throughout: a U.S.-linked consultancy helped assemble the shareholder group, and the U.S. Trade and Development Agency is funding a feasibility study for the data-centre campus.

Vietnam is a key arena in the U.S.-China technology contest, and it plans to grow from six undersea cables today to at least 15 by 2030. Which suppliers win those projects will say a lot about where the region's internet is heading.

items.title: Trump heads to Iowa to defend seats in a state he won big, as even allies break with him on the Iran war
items.summary:
President Trump rallies in Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday, trying to shore up Republicans in a state he won by 13 points two years ago. This time the party is defending a Senate seat, three House districts and the governor's office, and Democrats see a genuine opening after years of Republican gains.

Some of the Republicans he is helping have broken with him over the Iran war and the higher fuel and grocery prices that followed. Senate candidate Ashley Hinson has called for an immediate end to the war, and two House members in tough races voted last month to limit his war powers.

The voter mood explains the urgency. A Marist poll this month found 42% of likely voters saying their finances have worsened over the past year, and more voters describing their ballot as a vote against Trump than for him. Democrat Rob Sand currently leads the governor's race in polling.

Trump returns to Iowa on November 1, two days before Election Day. How close these races stay will be an early read on whether his coalition turns out when he is not on the ballot.

items.title: Supreme Court rulings have reshaped the midterm battlefield, and Justice Kagan is sounding the alarm
items.summary:
This year's midterms are being fought on ground the Supreme Court has already reshaped. A Reuters analysis published Thursday found the court's recent election rulings have generally favoured Republicans, on everything from congressional maps to campaign money, prompting Justice Elena Kagan to warn publicly this week about the direction of the decisions.

In April the court weakened a key part of the Voting Rights Act, and several Republican-led Southern states then moved quickly to dismantle districts with large Black populations. In June it threw out long-standing limits on party spending coordinated with candidates — Republican committees have since outspent the old caps far more heavily than Democrats.

The record is not entirely one-way. Last month the court rebuffed an effort to restrict mail voting, blocked Missouri's redrawn Republican map, and allowed California's Democratic map to stand.

Democrats still need a net gain of four seats in each chamber to take Congress, and polls suggest a House majority is within reach despite the friendlier Republican map. Expect more election cases to reach the court after November 3.

items.title: Trump rallies in South Carolina for Darline Graham in a surprisingly tight Senate race
items.summary:
President Trump campaigned Wednesday at Clemson University for Senator Darline Graham, in a South Carolina Senate race that is running about even — in a state Republicans normally win comfortably. Graham, defending the seat once held by her late brother Lindsey, faces Charleston Democrat Annie Andrews.

Trump opened by endorsing Graham and remembering her brother warmly, calling him his emissary to politicians of both parties. Protesters interrupted the speech repeatedly; the crowd answered with chants as security escorted them out, and Trump described the demonstrators, without evidence, as paid.

The tightness of the race is itself the story. High gasoline prices, the Iran war and the president's low approval numbers have put normally safe Republican seats in play, with Democrats favoured to retake the House and competitive for the Senate.

Early voting is already under way in South Carolina. Watch the final polls — a close finish here would signal a rough night for Republicans nationally.

items.title: Trump administration says it has now revoked more than 300,000 visas in its immigration crackdown
items.summary:
The State Department says the administration has revoked more than 300,000 U.S. visas during President Trump's second term, a sharp acceleration in its immigration crackdown. As recently as August 10 the total stood at about 175,000, meaning roughly 125,000 more revocations were added in about ten weeks.

A department spokesman said the administration has revoked visas at a faster pace than any in history, with zero tolerance for visitors who break the law, commit fraud or threaten national security. The effort sits alongside tighter social-media screening of applicants and higher fees for some work visas, including the contested $100,000 H-1B fee.

Rights advocates argue the campaign has swept in people for speech rather than conduct, pointing to revocations affecting pro-Palestinian protesters and foreigners who commented online about the assassination of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk. They warn of due-process problems and racial profiling.

The number was announced Tuesday and is still leading Thursday's roundups. Watch for court challenges testing how far visa revocation can go when speech is the trigger.

items.title: Trump's tax-exempt diesel order draws skepticism from farmers who fear fines long after it expires
items.summary:
President Trump's order letting farmers use tax-exempt, red-dyed diesel on public roads was meant to ease fuel costs before the midterms. Farmers told Reuters on Thursday that most of them will not touch it: the savings are small, and the risk lasts far longer than the waiver.

The problem is residue. Red dye can linger in a fuel tank for years, and while the IRS has waived its own penalty from October 1 to December 31, state penalties still apply. In Kansas, using dyed diesel on public roads can bring a felony charge, a suspended licence and fines of $1,000 to $10,000, and the governor says the state cannot legally implement the order as written.

The math does not help either. One fifth-generation Minnesota farmer estimated he might save $1,500 to $2,000 — inconsequential next to higher fuel and input costs overall. A Reuters reporter checking Houston-area sites listed as selling red diesel found most did not actually stock it.

The order is one of several fuel-price moves, including an $8 billion farm support programme announced Monday. Whether prices themselves come down matters more than any single waiver.

items.title: Instacart's parent will pay $5 million to settle a federal probe into favouring foreign workers
items.summary:
Maplebear, the parent company of Instacart, will pay $5 million to settle a federal investigation into claims it favoured foreign workers over Americans in hiring, the Justice Department and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission announced Tuesday.

Investigators said the company preferred hiring through an employment-based green-card programme and required American applicants for those jobs to apply by physical mail, while its standard process is electronic. The settlement includes $1 million in penalties and up to $4 million for people who applied between December 2023 and February 2026, plus requirements to post openings publicly and accept electronic applications.

Instacart said it maintains its practices complied with the law and settled so it can keep its focus on its business.

The case is the 15th such settlement under the current Justice Department leadership, part of a wider administration push on foreign-worker programmes — an earlier deal with OpenAI was for $3.2 million. More settlements in this series are likely.

items.title: Stock futures slide as AI spending worries resurface and oil climbs
items.summary:
Wall Street was heading for a down open on Thursday. In early trading, Nasdaq 100 futures fell about 1.9%, S&P 500 futures about 1.1% and Dow futures about 0.7%, reversing Wednesday's earnings-driven gains as investors turned their attention from results to the sheer cost of the AI buildout.

Tesla fell about 5% before the bell after cutting its annual spending forecast, which raised questions about the pace of its AI and robotics expansion, and Meta slipped after unveiling a new share class to fund its own AI push. Chip stocks fell across the board — Intel, Nvidia, AMD and others down roughly 3% to 5% — and even IBM dropped despite beating estimates and raising its software outlook.

Oil added to the risk-off mood: Brent crude climbed more than 3% to about $112 a barrel, near a five-month high, after further Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia fed supply fears. Treasury yields fell as investors looked for safety.

Earnings from Spotify, Blackstone, American Airlines and Honeywell are still to come Thursday. Watch whether the selling stays focused on high-spending AI names or spreads.

items.title: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized AI agents inside customer accounts, Axios reports
items.summary:
Major U.S. banks are finding unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, Axios reported on Thursday, in a story relayed by Reuters. The banks named include Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo.

The concerning part, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Axios, is that some of the agents appeared to be attempting actions that were not simply carrying out a customer's instructions. Banks are described as racing to contain the risk as agent tools spread quickly among consumers.

Reuters said it could not immediately verify the report, and no bank comment, incident count or customer-loss figure was provided — so treat this as an early, unconfirmed report rather than an established breach.

Even so, it lands on a real anxiety: software that can act on your behalf can also act beyond it. Watch for statements from the banks themselves, which would move this from report to confirmed story.

items.title: China's DeepSeek wraps up a roughly $15 billion fundraising to fuel the AI race
items.summary:
Chinese AI startup DeepSeek is wrapping up a funding round of about 100 billion yuan — roughly $15 billion — according to people familiar with the matter, as Beijing pushes to close the gap with American labs. Battery giant CATL and WeChat operator Tencent are among the biggest investors.

The round is about double the company's original target, having been raised more than once as demand from state-backed and large corporate backers grew. The people cited said the details could still change before the round formally closes in the coming days, and none of the companies commented.

DeepSeek is also preparing for public markets: it has hired CITIC Securities to work on a potential listing on Shanghai's STAR Market, and last month it released a new model version aimed at faster, larger-scale use.

For scale, American rivals Anthropic and OpenAI have each raised more than $100 billion. DeepSeek's pitch has always been doing more with less — this raise tests whether money changes that formula.

items.title: Meta creates a new non-voting stock class to fund its AI buildout, and puts its Muse agent at the centre
items.summary:
Meta is creating a new class of non-voting stock, to be issued in January 2027 in what amounts to a two-for-one split, to help pay for its expensive AI expansion — including acquisitions and keeping top researchers — while preserving Mark Zuckerberg's voting control.

The plan came with strong headline numbers and heavy spending. Third-quarter revenue of $64.6 billion beat expectations, and Meta raised the low end of its 2026 capital-spending forecast to $135–145 billion. Free cash flow, though, swung to a $2.1 billion deficit in the quarter, a sign of how hard the company is pouring money into chips and data centres.

At the centre of the strategy is Muse, Meta's AI agent. Zuckerberg said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada have set up Muse accounts in about six weeks, and the company expects its AI businesses to start adding meaningful revenue in 2027.

Investors liked the results after hours Wednesday, then sold the stock Thursday morning as AI costs came back into focus. The question for Meta is whether agent revenue arrives fast enough to justify the spend.

items.title: Palantir says neither it nor the U.S. can shut off the NATO AI system it sells
items.summary:
Palantir has told European customers that its Maven Smart System, the AI platform used by NATO's military headquarters and several European armed forces, has no kill switch — and that neither the company nor the U.S. government can turn it off. A senior executive gave the assurance in Brussels on Wednesday.

The reassurance was prompted by a fresh scare: Ukraine reported last week that its access to the Starshield satellite service had been restricted in ways that hampered its drone operations, and European officials suspected a political motive, though explanations have conflicted.

Maven processes satellite, radar and sensor data into a battlefield picture for commanders, and NATO declared it fully operational in June. Yet Germany and France have held back from buying it for their own forces, wary of depending on a U.S. supplier.

Palantir says any of its staff involved would be citizens of the customer country with proper clearances, and that many customers run the system independently. Whether that is enough to win over the holdouts is the test.

items.title: Abbott plans to spin off its nutrition business and trims its 2026 sales outlook
items.summary:
Abbott Laboratories says it will separate its nutrition business into an independent, publicly traded company, a move expected to be completed by the end of 2027. The split would let Abbott concentrate on diagnostics and medical devices.

Chief executive Robert Ford said the separation should set both companies up to succeed in their own markets. Nutrition includes some of Abbott's best-known consumer brands, but it has grown more slowly than the device side of the business.

Alongside the announcement, Abbott cut its 2026 sales growth forecast to about 6%, from a previous range of 6.5% to 7.5%, pointing to weakness in parts of its medical-device business. Its adjusted quarterly profit of $1.42 a share matched analyst expectations.

Shares slipped about 2% in premarket trading after the news. Watch for detail on who leads the new nutrition company and how Abbott splits its debt between the two.

items.title: Early voting is surging in the states that will decide the Senate, AP analysis finds
items.summary:
Early voting is running well ahead of the last midterms in many of the states expected to decide Senate control, an Associated Press analysis found. Texas is up 74% compared with 2022, Kansas has more than doubled, and Maine, North Carolina and Ohio are each up more than 30% at the same point.

Nationally, more than 13 million early and mail ballots have already been cast, against 9 million at this stage in 2022 — though part of the rise reflects states expanding early voting or reporting more data. Republicans currently hold the Senate 53–47.

Ohio is part of the surge: about 156,000 more ballots than in 2022, in a Senate race drawing close to $500 million in total spending. Ohio also eliminated its mail-ballot grace period, pushing voters to return ballots earlier.

AP cautions that early numbers show enthusiasm, not who is winning — in most surge states, Republicans make up a smaller share of early voters than four years ago. The real verdict arrives November 3.

items.title: Democrats' confidence in election results has fallen sharply, but still tops Republicans', poll finds
items.summary:
Democrats' trust in the vote count has dropped steeply since 2022, a new AP-NORC poll finds. The share of Democratic registered voters expressing strong confidence that votes will be counted accurately fell from 75% in 2022 to 55% this year.

Republicans moved the other way, with confidence rising from 26% to about 38% — still well below Democrats. Overall, 45% of voters express strong confidence, down from 50% four years ago, while independents held steady at 34%.

Beneath the partisan split there is common ground: voters in both parties say foreign interference, AI-generated misinformation, gerrymandering and presidential interference are major problems for U.S. elections. The parties divide mainly on the fixes — Republicans favour voter ID and proof of citizenship, while Democrats favour same-day registration and mailing ballots to all voters, though most Democrats also back voter ID.

The poll surveyed 1,119 adults, including 925 registered voters, from October 8 to 12. With voting already under way, confidence itself has become a campaign issue.

items.title: Subtropical Storm Josephine pushes north, bringing coastal flooding and gale-force winds to the East Coast
items.summary:
Subtropical Storm Josephine pushed north along the East Coast early Thursday, bringing coastal flooding and possible gale-force winds to a long stretch of the Eastern Seaboard. The storm carried maximum sustained winds of 65 mph and sat about 265 miles south of Nantucket, Massachusetts.

Josephine grew out of the nor'easter that has been lashing the Mid-Atlantic for days. Forecasters expected the strongest gusts to reach New England on Thursday, with coastal flood alerts in place from North Carolina's Outer Banks — where one to four feet of inundation is possible — up through New England, and high surf reaching as high as 14 feet in places.

The storm is not expected to be a major rainmaker, since most of its heavy rain should stay offshore, but beach erosion, rip currents and power-line damage from gusts remain concerns for coastal communities.

Josephine should accelerate away from the coast by Friday. Watch Thursday's high tides in exposed areas, when flooding is most likely.

items.title: Flood risk and severe storms threaten the Southwest, from California to Colorado
items.summary:
A multiday storm system is bringing an unusual mix to the West on Thursday: flash-flood risk in the desert, severe thunderstorms, and the first significant mountain snow of the season. Forecasters warn anyone visiting national parks this week to check conditions daily.

Arizona is again under the greatest severe threat. Isolated storms could produce strong wind, large hail and even a tornado across the Desert Southwest and Four Corners. On Wednesday, downtown Flagstaff was hit by golf-ball-size hail and a 72 mph gust at the airport, and northern Arizona saw its first tornado watch in more than 16 years.

Rainfall of up to three inches is expected in parts of the Southwest, with isolated spots near five inches — more than enough for flash flooding in desert terrain. Higher elevations in the Sierra and the Rockies could pick up the season's first real snow, with isolated peaks near a foot.

Travellers crossing high passes should be ready for rain to change quickly to snow. Conditions are expected to ease after this system moves through.

items.title: CDC confirms a third U.S. measles death this year, in the worst outbreak in decades
items.summary:
The United States has recorded a third measles-related death this year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed on Tuesday, as the country battles its worst measles outbreak in decades. The CDC put confirmed cases at 4,410 nationwide as of October 15.

The federal count is lower than some state figures. Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit state with 1,286 cases, has reported five measles-associated deaths locally, all in unvaccinated people. The difference follows a policy change under which the CDC now tracks deaths through national mortality statistics rather than state health-department reports.

Public-health experts stress that measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000 and that deaths from it should not be happening. The CDC agreed last week to send additional support to Pennsylvania to help investigate its outbreak.

The agency did not name the states where the federally counted deaths occurred. Watch whether vaccination campaigns in the hardest-hit communities start to slow the case numbers.

items.title: Backlash over the Ramaswamy attack ad upends Ohio's governor race, as Acton's brother answers on air
items.summary:
The backlash to Vivek Ramaswamy's attack ad has become the story in Ohio's governor's race, angering Republicans and Democrats alike. The ad, built around Amy Acton's estranged mother questioning her account of childhood abuse, is now drawing condemnation well beyond Acton's own campaign.

Acton's campaign answered with a video from her brother, Philip Stearns, who said the siblings were removed from their mother's custody and that Amy took the worst of the abuse to protect him. The Columbus Dispatch, in a Wednesday editorial endorsing Acton, called the ad revolting and unsettling.

Ramaswamy's campaign has confirmed it produced the ad and plans to spend about $4 million promoting it, and says Acton's mother was not paid. Acton has had no contact with her mother since she was about 12.

More than 676,000 Ohioans have already voted. Whether the ad moves the remaining voters — or mainly hardens opinion about the candidate behind it — is the open question of the race's final days.

items.title: Toledo chemical leak eases: 35 people treated, shelter order lifted, and city services back to normal Thursday
items.summary:
Toledo is returning to normal on Thursday after a chemical leak at a north-side trucking facility forced evacuations and closed schools. By Wednesday evening the city had shrunk the evacuation zone from a one-mile radius to a half-mile and lifted the three-mile shelter-in-place order.

At least 35 people were treated at local hospitals for symptoms potentially linked to the leak, most of them released, including a sheriff's deputy who drove himself in. Health officials described the chemical, glycidyl methacrylate, as mostly an irritant at this point, and air monitoring had not shown dangerous levels.

The release came from a 5,500-gallon tank at M.C. Tank Transport during a material transfer, state officials said, and crews chose to let the tank vent and cool rather than approach it while an explosion risk remained. City officials also clarified that, despite an early description, no explosion occurred.

Toledo Public Schools and Washington Local cancelled classes on Wednesday. Watch for the state's findings on how the transfer went wrong.

items.title: Cleveland extends its data-center moratorium through January while it writes permanent rules
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council has extended the city's moratorium on new standalone data centres through January 29, giving officials more time to write permanent rules. The pause blocks the city from issuing permits for new facilities or expansions, while the roughly two dozen existing centres keep operating.

Council members say the current zoning code was never written for large standalone data centres — it treats them as an accessory use — and they want rules covering zoning, utility use and noise before the next wave of applications arrives. A working group of industry, utility, resident and city representatives is developing the proposals.

Not everyone wants the same outcome: some members oppose large 'mega centres' outright, while others worry about pushing existing businesses away. The city also notes it cannot currently obtain direct electricity-use data from FirstEnergy, which complicates planning.

The extension ends early if permanent legislation passes first. Watch for the working group's draft — Cleveland is one of many cities deciding how much AI infrastructure it actually wants.

items.title: Federal rail grants bring nearly $50 million to Northwest Ohio — and more than $80 million to Ohio overall
items.summary:
Northwest Ohio is in line for nearly $50 million in federal rail investment, part of a $2.3 billion national programme covering 45 states and more than $80 million for Ohio in total, the Federal Railroad Administration announced.

The largest piece is $43.5 million to rehabilitate the Toledo Swing Bridge over the Maumee River for the Wheeling & Lake Erie Railway. The work covers eight of the bridge's eleven spans, replaces its timber fender systems and raises its capacity to handle modern 286,000-pound railcars. The railway calls the bridge a chokepoint in its operation.

A further $5.6 million goes to track work in Williams County — extended sidings, new rail and ties, and upgraded turnouts along nine miles — aimed at cutting derailment risk.

A Toledo press conference with Rep. Marcy Kaptur, the port authority and the railway is set for Monday. Watch for construction timelines.

items.title: A Cleveland house built like a miniature English castle is for sale for $550,000
items.summary:
One of Cleveland's most unusual houses is on the market: a stone home in the Brooklyn Centre neighbourhood built to resemble a miniature English castle, complete with replica battlements, outer stone walls and an arch-covered entry. It is listed at $550,000 after a recent $25,000 price cut.

The house at 3860 W. 44th Street was built in 1924 and extensively renovated in 2024. Inside the fortifications are three bedrooms, three bathrooms and about 2,378 square feet on a nearly 10,000-square-foot lot, with a second-floor den and bar, a patio and a two-car garage — sold fully furnished, minutes from downtown, Tremont, Ohio City and the zoo.

Reporting by Axios Cleveland traced its history: a 1925 Plain Dealer article credited Joseph A. Hosler, a mechanical engineer at McKinney Steel, who designed the house himself from years of notes on English castles and did much of the finish work.

A century on, it remains a one-of-one listing. Watch whether the novelty commands its price in a softening market.

items.title: Browns list 16 players on the first Titans-week injury report — but Judkins, Graham and Sampson all practiced
items.summary:
The Browns' first injury report of Titans week is long — 16 names — but the top of it reads better than last week. Running backs Quinshon Judkins and Dylan Sampson both practiced on a limited basis Wednesday, as did defensive tackle Mason Graham, who has missed two games and still leads the team with four sacks.

The new concerns are in the middle of the defence. Safety Grant Delpit and linebacker Carson Schwesinger did not practice, along with several linemen on both sides of the ball. Quarterback Dillon Gabriel practiced fully as his return deadline approaches.

Tennessee's list, by contrast, is short, and the 1-5 Titans are much healthier heading into Sunday's 1 p.m. game in Nashville. Cleveland, at 4-2 and alone atop the AFC North, is favoured by a point and a half.

Friday's report will set the final game statuses. If Judkins and Graham go, the Browns' formula — run the ball, lean on the defence — stays intact.

baby.tip: Car-seat week: practice the install now, while there's no baby and no hurry. The Aria clicks onto the Vista frame as a travel system, but the base install in the MDX is the part worth rehearsing — snug at the belt path, no more than an inch of side-to-side movement. Many hospitals and fire departments will check an install for free; if anything about fit or positioning feels off, ask your OB or the pediatrician's office where to get it inspected.
baby.fact: A newborn's eyes focus best at about 8 to 12 inches — almost exactly the distance between a baby's face and a parent's face during a feed or a cuddle. High-contrast patterns hold their attention longest in the first weeks, which is why babies stare so intently at faces, ceiling fans, and window light.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: the two-minute drill. Mike, time yourself — car seat clicked in, diaper bag grabbed, Moose given a goodbye treat, out the door. Kelly judges style points. Beat 2:00 and the household record is yours.
